incidente.resumo: Starting 1 April 2014 at 21:00 UTC, all GLONASS satellites transmitted wrong broadcast ephemerides, with satellite position errors up to about ±200 km, which the authors state were probably caused by a software update; about 60 of 180 IGS receivers used by CODE were severely affected, some also losing GPS tracking. The correction took place satellite by satellite from 22:45 UT, and all satellites transmitted correct messages again by 07:00 UTC on 2 April.

descricao.texto: The error was identified by the GLONASS provider almost immediately after the new broadcast ephemerides were activated; the text does not say how.
trechos: identified by the GLONASS provider almost immediately after the activation of the new BE …

descricao.texto: The failure was caused by wrong broadcast ephemerides transmitted simultaneously from all GLONASS satellites from 1 April 2014, 21:00 UTC, whose positions showed a consistent rotation of about 0.5 degrees about the inertial x-axis; the authors state this was probably caused by a software update activated at 9 p.m. UTC on 1 April.
trechos: The failure was caused by wrong Broadcast Ephemerides
probably caused by a software update, activated on April 1st at 9h p.m. UTC (24h/0h “Moscow Time”)
April 1, 21:00     GLONASS starts transmitting “infected” Broadcast messages simultaneously from all satellites.

Bad Broadcast Messages (resulting in satellite position errors up to about ±200km) were sent out starting April 1, 2014, 21h UT; Errors in geocentric, Earth-fixed x-coordinate of satellites of orbital plane 1.
Erroneous GLONASS Broadcast positions show a consistent rotation of about 0.5 degrees about inertial x-axis.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The error was identified by the GLONASS provider almost immediately but was not communicated to the users of GLONASS.
trechos: identified by the GLONASS provider almost immediately after the activation of the new BE …
but not communicated to the users of GLONASS.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The effect on receivers depended on receiver type and firmware release: some receivers were unaffected, some stopped tracking GLONASS after 9 p.m. and some even stopped GPS tracking.
trechos: The effect on receivers obviously was dependent on the receiver type & firmware release.
Some receivers unaffected, some stopped tracking GLONASS after 9h p.m. (red line), some even stopped GPS tracking!

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The broadcast ephemerides are a single point of failure for the IGS Real-time Experiment, which sends out corrections relative to them.
trechos: The BE are, however, of vital importance for the IGS Real-time Service (corrections w.r.t. BE are sent out); the BE are a “single point of failure” for the IGS real-time Experiment.

descricao.texto: The authors state the wrong broadcast ephemerides were probably caused by a software update activated on 1 April at 9 p.m. UTC; the update is not identified further.
trechos: probably caused by a software update, activated on April 1st at 9h p.m. UTC (24h/0h “Moscow Time”)

passos.texto: The correction (the authors ask whether it was a switch back to the old software release) took place satellite by satellite starting on 1 April at 10:45 p.m. UT; all GLONASS satellites transmitted correct broadcast messages again by 2 April, 7:00 UTC, satellite 21 being the last.
trechos: The correction (switch back to “old” software release?) took place satellite-by-satellite (starting on April 1, 10h45m p.m. UT).
April 2, 7:00        All GLONASS satellites transmit again correct broadcast messages (satellite 21 last satellite).

acoes.texto: Recommendation to the IGS: either implement an IGS real-time validation of all broadcast ephemerides of all GNSS and make it available to users, or reconsider the use of the broadcast ephemerides for the IGS Real-time Experiment.
trechos: implement an IGS real-time validation of all BE of all GNSS and make it available to the user community.
reconsider the use of the BE for the IGS Real-time Experiment, as well.

acoes.texto: Recommendation to the IGS: before combination, determine parameters of general interest (e.g. station coordinates, Earth Rotation Parameters) separately using only GPS or only GLONASS observations, so GNSS-specific problems are identified more easily; receiver software/firmware should follow the same principle.
trechos: Prior to combination, parameters of general interest (e.g., station coordinates, Earth Rotation Parameters) should be determined separately using only the observations of either GPS or GLONASS.
GNSS-specific problems are more easily identified this way.
The same principle should be observed by receiver software/firmware.

acoes.texto: Recommendation to the IGS: monitor the quality of the broadcast ephemerides of all GNSS, possibly using the predicted part of the IGS ultra-rapid orbits.
trechos: In addition, the quality of BE of all GNSS should be monitored by the IGS. For that purpose the predicted part of the IGS ultra-rapid orbits might be used.

acoes.texto: Recommendation to the IGS: reports about malfunctioning receivers might be collected routinely and made available in a report.
trechos: Report about malfunctioning receivers might be collected routinely and made available in a report.
April 1, 21:00     GLONASS starts transmitting “infected” Broadcast messages simultaneously from all satellites.
April 2, 7:00        All GLONASS satellites transmit again correct broadcast messages (satellite 21 last satellite).

perguntas_em_aberto: Whether the satellite-by-satellite correction was a switch back to the old software release (the text marks this with a question mark).

observacoes: The document is a conference presentation by IGS-affiliated researchers analysing the GLONASS event from outside; the prevention items are recommendations the authors give to the IGS (and receiver software/firmware), not commitments of the GLONASS provider. duracao is computed from the chronicle of events (21:00 to 07:00 UTC); some slides say transmission was back to normal 'around 6h UT of April 2', and satellites 6, 7, 8, 14, 15, 23 and 24 were back to normal before the end of 1 April. The authors state IGS post-processing products were virtually not affected because orbits use one day of observations and only about 1/3 of GLONASS tracking data was missing. They also note that at the time of the transition back to normal the satellites were visible from at least one Command Tracking Site on Russian territory.
